LESSON: CHEMICAL BONDING

Grade: SNE  /  visual-impairment / Grade 10
Subject: CHEMISTRY FOR LEARNERS WITH VISUAL IMPAIRMENT JUNE
Strand: Inorganic chemistry
Topic 1.4: Chemical Bonding
Suggested lessons in curriculum: 26

SECTION 1: INTRODUCTION

This lesson covers Chemical Bonding, part of Inorganic chemistry in SNE  /  visual-impairment / Grade 10 CHEMISTRY FOR LEARNERS WITH VISUAL IMPAIRMENT JUNE.

Key inquiry question: How do chemical bonds influence the properties of substances?

You will study the official KICD learning outcomes, classroom activities, values, and competencies for this topic. Use Kenyan examples from your county, school, and community throughout.

SECTION 2: LEARNING OUTCOMES

By the end of this topic, you should be able to:

A. illustrate bond types in elements, molecules and ● In groups, learners review the concept of stability of atoms (gaining and/or losing electrons), How do chemical bonds influence the properties of substances? 14 compounds (for learners with low vision), b) interpret tactile graphics of bond types in elements, molecules and compounds (for learners with blindness), c) investigate the relationship between bond types and physical properties of elements, molecules and compounds, d) relate bond types and resultant structures to the uses of elements, molecules and compounds, e) appreciate the uses of different substances based on their bond types and structures in day to day life. ● In groups, learners discuss the role of valence electrons in bonding (octet/duplet noble gas configuration), ● Learners discuss with peers different types of chemical bonds (ionic, covalent, dative covalent, hydrogen bond, Van der Waals forces and metallic), ● In pairs, learners with low vision are guided to draw Lewis structures dot (.) and/or cross (x) diagrams to show bonding in selected elements, molecules and compounds. Learners with blindness are guided to manipulate and explore tactile graphics showing bonding in selected elements, molecules and compounds (ionic, covalent, dative covalent, 15 hydrogen bond, Van der Waals forces and metallic bonding), ● in groups, learners are guided to carry out activities to investigate the physical properties of giant ionic, simple molecular, giant atomic/covalent and giant metallic compounds (solubility, thermal and electrical conductivity, melting point, boiling point).Learners with blindness to tactually examine the apparatus and materials of the experiment before, during and after the procedure to familiarise. They should also be involved in assembling the apparatus and make tactual and auditory observations such as feeling the heat and hearing the sound buzzers 16 for demonstrating electrical conductivity in addition to verbal descriptions of observations that exclusively require sight such as dissolving ionic compounds in water, ● learners to watch or listen to audio visual animations or simulations on chemical bonding and resultant structures, ● learners brainstorm the relationship between bond type and physical properties of elements and compounds (diamond, graphite, sodium chloride, aluminium metal, among others), ● in groups, learners are guided to use braille, print media references or digital devices with assistive technology to explore uses 17 of elements, molecules and compounds based on their bond types and structures. SECTION 4: LEARNING ACTIVITIES

A. At school

Follow your teacher’s guidance for group work, discussion, and practice on this topic.

B. At home with your parent or guardian

1. Read this lesson on Chemical Bonding together.
2. Discuss the key inquiry question and give examples from your area.
3. Write five sentences summarising what you learned.
4. Prepare for the revision quiz at the end of this topic.

SECTION 5: CORE COMPETENCIES, VALUES, AND PCIs

Core Competencies to be developed:
● Learning to learn: the learner with low vision learns dependently while drawing dot and cross diagrams to illustrate

bonding in elements and compounds

● Digital literacy: the learner uses digital devices with assistive technology to effectively accomplish own task while

watching animations, simulations, and videos on chemical bonding.

● Creativity and Imagination: The learner experiments with material to develop models to illustrate bonding in selected

elements/compounds using locally available materials.

● Critical Thinking and Problem Solving: The learner interprets and infer with peers the relationship between bond

types and resulting structures.

Values:
Love: the learner shows care by avoiding to hurt others as they carry out activities to investigate the physical properties

of different structures.

18

Pertinent and Contemporary Issues:
(PCIs)

● Socio-Economic and Environmental issues (Environment conservation): The learner uses locally available materials

to make models.

● Life skills (creative thinking): The learner models bonding in selected elements/compounds e.g., SiO2, NaCl,

graphite and diamond.

● Socio-Economic and Environmental issues (social cohesion): The learner discusses with peers different types of

chemical bonds.

Suggested Learning Resources:

Print and braille version of the periodic table, 3-D models of the periodic table, braille labelling tape, manilla papers,

markers, digitals devices with assistive technology, basic laboratory apparatus and reagents, tactile versions of lab

equipment such as such as talking scales, tactile measuring devices, adapted syringes, beakers and graduated cylinders,

3-D models of different types of bonds and structures such graphite, diamond silicon (IV) oxide and sodium chloride.

Suggested Key Skill(s)

• Investigate the relationship between bond types and physical properties of elements.

• Relate bond types and resultant structures to the uses of elements, molecules and compound.
